content: Cholera is a severe diarrheal disease that can lead to death if not treated promptly. It is particularly prevalent in areas with poor sanitation, such as refugee camps. Over the past 50 years, several vaccines have been developed to prevent cholera. This review focuses on oral vaccines made from killed bacteria and evaluates their effectiveness and safety, specifically those prequalified by the World Health Organization (WHO). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effectiveness and safety of WHO-prequalified oral killed cholera vaccines. Participants of all ages and sexes were included, and the studies were conducted in various settings. The control groups in these trials received either a placebo, another vaccine, or no vaccine at all. The outcomes measured were related to the vaccines' ability to prevent cholera and their safety profiles. Five RCTs, involving a total of 462,754 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These trials evaluated two types of oral killed cholera vaccines: the whole-cell plus recombinant vaccine (WC-rBS, marketed as Dukoral) and the bivalent whole-cell vaccine (BivWC, marketed as Shanchol). The trials were conducted in Peru, India, and Bangladesh. No trials were identified for other BivWC vaccines, such as Euvichol/Euvichol-Plus or Hillchol. Two doses of Dukoral, with or without a booster dose, were shown to reduce cholera cases by 76% at two years of follow-up in a general population of children and adults. In adult males, the vaccine was effective for up to five months. This finding is supported by high-certainty evidence. Two doses of Shanchol were found to reduce cholera cases by 37% at one year of follow-up, 64% at two years, and 80% at five years. These results are supported by highto moderate-certainty evidence, depending on the follow-up period. A single dose of Shanchol was also effective, reducing cholera cases by 40% at six months and 39% at two years of follow-up. Additionally, a single dose reduced cases of severe dehydrating cholera by 63% at six months and 50% at two years. These findings are supported by high-certainty evidence. No significant differences in adverse events were observed between the vaccine and control groups, indicating that the vaccines are safe and well-tolerated. In conclusion, two doses of Dukoral are effective in reducing cholera cases for up to two years, while two doses of Shanchol provide protection for up to five years. A single dose of Shanchol also offers significant protection for up to two years. Although no trials were conducted on other BivWC vaccines like Euvichol/Euvichol-Plus, these products are considered to produce similar immune responses to Shanchol. Therefore, the results from Shanchol trials can reasonably be applied to these other vaccines.
